title: Man United announce a change of scapegoat
text:
Man United announce a change of scapegoat 
 Skip to content 
 Man United announce a change of scapegoat
 The people who chose Pochettino are the same ones who thought Carrick was the answer in May and then changed the question by November
 Opinion 
 Comment 
 Sport 
 Football 
 15 November 2026 
 | 
 James Calvert 
 | Comments: 
 6 min read
 What Mauricio Pochettino will inherit is a Frankenstein’s monster of a squad, assembled for half a dozen managers who wanted to play half a dozen different ways. PHOTO: Kevin C. Cox/Getty Images/AFP 
 If there were any justice in the world, it would have been Michael Carrick sacking Manchester United last week and not the other way round. 
 He could have called the club in on Thursday morning, thanked it for its efforts and told it that, after a disappointing start to the season, he’d decided a change was necessary if he was going to achieve his ambitions. 
 Sadly, real life doesn’t work that way round.
 In May, United gave Carrick a contract until 2028 after he took over in January, got them up to third and put them back in the Champions League. On Wednesday he turned up for work at Carrington and by lunchtime the rest of us were reading that United had agreed a deal in principle with Mauricio Pochettino. 
 On Thursday, they sacked him and called him a club legend, which is a title you would generally expect to earn you a somewhat more dignified exit. 
 Yes, one win in 10 league games is dreadful, and 18th is a ridiculous place for Manchester United to be. But, as I said last week, I still believe he had earned the chance to turn things around. 
 Last week his team came from two down to beat Roma, and then scored twice in stoppage time to draw 4-4 with Aston Villa. The defending was dreadful, but there was enough fight in those two games to suggest the players were still playing for him.
 And even if you think United were right to sack him, the way they went about it was despicable.
 The rot at United starts at the top and works its way down 
 On the other hand, I like Pochettino. He did excellent work at Southampton and took Tottenham to a Champions League final. He’s been on United’s wish list for so long that I’d begun to assume the job would eventually pass to him by default.
 The Argentinian could well turn out to be the right man for the right job at the right time. But I can’t help feel we have said the same about the last few men who have tried and failed to resurrect this comatose giant. 
 What he’ll inherit is a Frankenstein’s monster of a squad, assembled for half a dozen managers who wanted to play half a dozen different ways. Every time United change direction, the players bought for the previous one are still there. The new bloke is expected to make sense of it all while the people who put the squad together sit upstairs wondering why the jigsaw pieces aren’t fitting. 
 As I’ve said before, the rot at United starts at the top and works its way down. Pochettino could do well if he’s given the time and backing to build a team in his own image. The trouble is that the people who’ll decide how much time he gets are the same ones who thought Carrick was the answer in May and then changed the question by November. 
 I wouldn’t wish relegation on United’s fans – they’ve had a crap enough time already. 
 But if there were a way to relegate Omar Berrada, Jason Wilcox, Jim Ratcliffe and the Glazers individually, I’d happily spend the rest of the season cheering them all the way to the bottom.
 I think Domino’s Pizza summed up the entire thing perfectly last week when they shared a post of Carrick being sacked and said that was like to trying to improve a ham and pineapple pizza by removing the ham.
 Couldn’t have put it better myself.
 Chengdu miss the point 
 The last time I saw anything collapse as quickly as Chengdu Rongcheng’s title challenge, I was halfway through stacking books on a shelf I’d just put up. 
 Chengdu were 14 points clear of Dalian Yingbo with five games left in the Chinese Super League. A draw in the first of those games left them needing one more point to be crowned champions. That’s four chances to play out the sort of goalless draw that makes you wish you’d stayed home putting up shelves. 
 They lost all four. 
 They even had a penalty at home to Dalian in the penultimate game. Felipe hit it close enough to the goalkeeper to spare him the inconvenience of having to choose which way to dive. Dalian won 1-0, which left Chengdu needing a draw at Shandong Taishan on the final day.
 They lost 3-2. 
 Meanwhile over the run-in, Dalian went on a run of five straight wins, including that one over their direct rivals. That meant they finished level with Chengdu on 52 points but took the title on head-to-head having beaten them twice.
 We’ve seen some good collapses in England. Arsenal watched an eight-point lead disappear in 2023, although the team chasing them was Pep Guardiola’s Manchester City, who went on to win the treble.
 And there’s the famous one in 1996, when Kevin Keegan’s Newcastle United were 12 points clear and still ended up watching Manchester United lift the trophy. Newcastle, in fairness, took several months to do what Chengdu managed in four games. 
 What I love about the Chengdu tale is how little they had to do. One grim afternoon of knocking the ball into the stands and taking an unreasonable amount of time over goal kicks would have done it. They could have bored their way into the history books. 
 Instead, here we are.
 When family ties go wrong 
 I don’t think I’ve ever seen anyone look quite as happy and quite as miserable at the same time as Robbie Savage did when his son Charlie scored against him in last weekend’s FA Cup. 
 I’ve watched the clip dozens of times and every time I think I’ve settled on what he’s feeling, his face changes its mind. There’s a flicker of a smile, then he looks like he might cry, and you genuinely wonder whether it’s possible to explode from an unexpected mix of pride and despair. 
 Watching it again just now, I still can’t decide whether he wants to punch the air or put his head in his hands. For a second he looks as though he might do both and accidentally punch himself in the face. 
 How did this come about? Well, Robbie manages Peterborough United and Charlie plays for Reading, and the draw put them up against each other in the first round. 
 Robbie said they’d gone the whole week without their usual chats because he didn’t want to put Charlie in a position where he might let something slip about Reading’s plans. And those plans apparently involved giving Peterborough a good spanking.
 Sure enough, Charlie scored Reading’s third and celebrated with a knee slide. Reading went on to win 5-0, which must have made family dinner rather awkward. 
 That goal is certainly a moment Savage senior will never forget. As a dad, you want to tell your son how proud you are of him. As a manager, you want to know who the bloody hell was supposed to be marking him.
